senses.gloss:
diggajas
(‘the elephants [that are supporting the] directions’)
------------------------------------------
As per the Hindu mythological accounts, this earth is being carried by eight elephants situated in the eight directions. Hence they are called ‘aṣṭa-दिग्गजस्’ or simply as ‘diggajas’. Each of the diks or directions has a protector or dikpāla (or dikpālaka) also and these elephants are under them.
Their names can be listed as follows:
dik or direction dikpāla diggaja
pūrva (east) Indra Airāvata
āgneya (south-east) Agni Puṇḍarīka
dakṣiṇa (south) Yama Vāmana
nairṛtya (south-west) Sūrya Kumuda
paścima (west) Varuṇa Añjana
vāyavya (north-west) Vāyu Puṣpadanta
uttara (north) Kubera Sārvabhauma
īśānya (north-east) Īśāna or Candra Supratīka

These elephants have their female consorts too like Abhramu, Kapilā, पिङ्गला and so on.
The Rāmāyaṇa (1.40) mentions only four दिग्गजस्. They are: Virūpākṣa (east), Mahāpadma (south), Sumanā (west) and Bhadra (north).

digvijaya
(‘conquering [in all] directions’)
------------------------------------------
Expeditions by ambitious kings for conquering others’ territories or for collecting ransoms from them have been known to exist right from the most ancient times. Such expeditions were called ‘dig-विजय’.
Kauṭilya’s Arthaśāstra (12.1) classifies such digvijayas into three kinds:—
dharmavijaya: Here the conqueror is satisfied if the defeated ruler agrees to be submissive.
lobhavijaya: The conqueror is satisfied if he gets land and money.
asuravijaya: This is the lowest and abominable type since the conqueror robs the vanquished king of all his possessions.
The dharmaśāstra works condemn the last one.

digbandhana
(‘shutting out [the evil spirits]’)
------------------------------------------
In ritualistic worship as also in any ritualistic act, especially those aimed at fulfilment of desires, there is always a possibility of obstacles being created by inimical spirits. These spirits have to be ‘locked out’ of dik (= quarters) during the ritual. The way of doing it is by chanting certain powerful mantras or mystical formulae like the व्याहृतिस् of the गायत्री or syllables like phaṭ. This is called ‘digbandhana’ or ‘digbandha’. After the ritual is over, the quarters (or dik) have to be reopened. This is called ‘digvimoka’.
The process may also be used to arrest the movements of those who are likely to harm a person, like criminals. Such use of extraordinary powers has been recorded in the lives of great saints like Tailaṅga Svāmin (19th century) and विजयदास (A. D. 1682-1755).
